title: Macramé dreamcatcher
subtitle: A spiral-knotted web in a metal ring, finished with cord and feather drops
excerpt: A macramé dreamcatcher is a circular metal or wooden ring filled with a knotted spiral web and finished with hanging cord drops and feathers. The finished piece is about 15 to 20 cm across the ring with drops of 20 to 30 cm below. The web is knotted directly onto the ring in a clockwise spiral.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from traditional macramé craft practice. The dreamcatcher form originates in Ojibwe tradition; the macramé interpretation using knotted cotton cord and metal rings is a modern craft adaptation widely taught in beginner workshops.

glossaryTerms.definition: A mounting knot used to attach cord to a ring or dowel. The cord is folded in half and both ends drawn through the loop formed at the midpoint.
A simple wrapping knot where the working cord passes over and under the filler cord and through its own loop. The foundation of the dreamcatcher web spiral.

content.text: A macramé dreamcatcher is built from a series of
knots spiralling inward around a metal ring. The work begins with

around the ring edge and then a single working cord completes the web by making a half-hitch around each successive loop from the previous round. The pattern shrinks as it spirals inward, leaving a small central hole at the finish. Use a 3 to 5 mm single-ply cotton cord in natural white or cream.

items.name: Metal or wooden ring, 15 to 20 cm diameter
3 mm single-strand cotton macramé cord in natural or dyed colour
Small feathers for drops (craft feathers or natural)
Optional: small wooden or glass beads for the drops

content.text: Wrap the ring with cord from start to finish to cover the metal or wood surface. This gives the web half-hitches a better surface to grip and gives the dreamcatcher a more finished look. Secure the wrapping at the start and end with a tight half-hitch. A 15 cm ring requires about 3 m of cord to wrap at a standard thickness.

Attach a long working cord to the ring with a lark's head knot at the top. Pass the cord clockwise around the ring, making an evenly spaced loop every 2 to 3 cm. Secure each loop to the ring with a half-hitch. For a 15 cm ring, space 8 to 10 loops evenly around the ring. The loops form the structure for the next round's half-hitches.

Without cutting the cord, continue clockwise and make a half-hitch around the middle of each loop from the first round. The second round of half-hitches sits inside the first, pulling the pattern toward the centre. Continue in this way, each round making half-hitches around the previous round's mid-points, until the web reaches the centre of the ring. Secure the end with a firm knot and trim.

Cut three to five lengths of cord, each about 30 cm, and attach them to the bottom of the ring with lark's head knots, evenly spaced. Thread beads if desired and secure with an overhand knot below each bead. Attach feathers at the end of each drop by folding a small length of cord around the feather quill and knotting it in place, or by tucking the quill into the last knot on the drop. Add a hanging loop of cord at the top of the ring.

items.problem: The web spirals unevenly and comes out lopsided
items.cause: The first-round loops were not evenly spaced around the ring, so the subsequent rounds do not line up concentrically
items.fix: Measure and mark the ring at equal intervals before starting the first round. Eight equally spaced loops at 45-degree intervals on a 15 cm ring produce a consistent web.

items.problem: The web cord runs out before reaching the centre
items.cause: The working cord was not long enough at the start
items.fix: For a 15 cm ring with 8 loops and five or six spiral rounds, allow at least 10 m of working cord. Add more cord by joining with an overhand knot at a half-hitch point, then trimming the knot short after the web is complete.
